title: The mountaintop
hook: the night before he is killed, King says he's seen the promised land

segments.voice: Yesterday: Birmingham, a letter written in the margins. Your line: justice is all one piece.

Rain and wind outside a church in Memphis. Sanitation workers in the city are on strike, carrying signs that say they are men, and Martin Luther King Jr. has come to stand with them. He's tired, with a sore throat. He nearly stays at the hotel, but the people waiting call him, and he comes. He speaks a long time: the strike, the Good Samaritan, the road ahead. Near the end, he talks about his own life, and how long it might be. The next evening, he is shot and killed on a motel balcony.

In the closing minutes, King said he had been to the mountaintop. He had looked over and seen the promised land. He might not get there with them, he said, but they, as a people, would get there. And he wasn't worried; he feared no one. Listeners who knew their Bibles would have heard where that came from. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses has led his people out of slavery and through the wilderness. He climbs to the top of Pisgah, and God shows him the whole land spread out below. Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Moses sees it, but doesn't enter. He dies there, and the people go on without him. King placed himself in that story, and it isn't a hopeless one. The letter to the Hebrews describes the old heroes of faith the same way: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them." Seeing from far off is still seeing. Hope, in this picture, doesn't depend on getting there yourself. King ended that night with the opening line of the Battle Hymn of the Republic: "Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord." Then he stepped back from the pulpit. Some listeners remember the speech for its strange calm: a man who sounds as if he senses what may be coming, and has made his peace with not crossing over.
screen: `MOSES ON PISGAH: SEE, BUT NOT ENTER.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you're part of that you may never see finished: a child growing up, a garden, a cause, a family healing slowly, a church, a town. Picture it from a height, the way Moses saw the land, not today's mess but the whole of it further on, without needing to arrive. If you pray, offer it to God as unfinished.
The mountaintop. King's last speech, in Memphis, where he said he had seen the promised land and might not get there with his people.
Your line: look toward the promised land. Seen afar off, and embraced. Day nine hundred sixty-one, done.

howItsDone: Some churches in the United States remember King's life and words near his birthday, and the mountaintop speech is sometimes played or read aloud at those services.

chat.says: King said he'd seen the promised land but might not get there. Was he giving up?
options: No. Like Moses on Pisgah, he saw it from afar, and hoped for his people without needing to arrive.
Yes. After so much struggle, he'd decided the promised land wasn't coming for anyone.
No. He meant he planned to step away from the movement and let younger leaders finish it.
chat.meaning: King echoed Moses, who saw the land but didn't enter. Hebrews says such people saw the promises afar off and embraced them: hope, not defeat.
